title: COMI: Context Compression via Information Gain
one_liner: To compress long documents for language models, keep the parts most relevant to the question and discard overlapping copies.
lead: When a language model reads a very long document, it slows down and gets confused by duplicate information. COMI solves this by measuring each piece of text on two scales: how useful it is for answering the question, and how much it overlaps with other pieces. The method drops the overlapping parts and adjusts how much to compress each section based on this measurement.

paras: Language models read one token (a small piece of text or a word) at a time. When the document is very long, the model has to look at every token and compare it to every other token to decide what is important. With a long document, this comparison step becomes extremely slow and memory-hungry.

A naive approach is to compress blindly, cutting out parts of the document without knowing which parts matter for the question. This loses critical information. A better naive approach is to keep only parts that sound related to the question, because the model's attention is drawn to query-related pieces. But natural language is repetitive: the same idea appears many times with slightly different wording. So you end up keeping similar parts and still storing the same information twice, wasting space even after compression.

callout.html: Keep the parts most relevant to the question, and merge the overlapping ones.

steps.text: Split the document into equal-sized chunks.
Compute MIG: relevance to the query minus overlap with other groups.
High-MIG groups keep more tokens; low-MIG groups compress heavily.
Combine redundant tokens using MIG weights so key ideas survive.
Model reads a much shorter input with no information loss.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: The paper changes how compression rates are assigned. Instead of compressing all sections equally, or compressing based only on relevance, COMI assigns each section its own compression rate based on a score called Marginal Information Gain. Sections that score high keep more tokens; sections that score low lose more tokens.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Marginal Information Gain
hidden.name: Marginal Information Gain (MIG)
paras: MIG is a score for each piece of text, defined as the relevance of that piece to the input query, minus how much it overlaps with other pieces. Relevance is measured by how much the model's attention focuses on that piece when answering the question. Redundancy (overlap) is measured by how similar the piece is to other pieces in meaning.
The paper uses MIG at two levels: between groups (to set compression rates), and within each group (to decide which tokens to merge). In both cases, high MIG means the piece is worth keeping.

heat.caption: Darker means higher MIG (more relevant, less redundant). Highlighted groups get lower compression rates.

reads.html: MIG tells you which pieces of the document are both useful for the question and unique (not repeated elsewhere).
MIG is defined as the relevance of a unit to the query minus its semantic redundancy with other units.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the causal chain
paras: The model's attention mechanism naturally focuses only on a small subset of tokens relevant to the query. If you compress without knowing which tokens those are, you risk deleting the ones the model depends on to answer the question. By measuring relevance via attention patterns, the method preserves the tokens the model actually needs.

Natural language is repetitive. Multiple sentences express the same idea with different words. If you keep only high-relevance tokens without checking for redundancy, you keep many similar copies of the same concept. By measuring redundancy and subtracting it from relevance, the method identifies tokens that are both important and unique. This means fewer tokens are kept overall, but no information is lost because the surviving tokens do not repeat.

By setting compression rates per group rather than globally, the method adapts to the structure of the text. Questions and definitions might be dense with unique information, so they keep most tokens. Supporting examples might be redundant, so they compress more. This fine-tuning under the same compression budget preserves more signal.

math.words: Marginal Information Gain = Relevance of a unit to the query minus Semantic overlap of that unit with other units
symbols: marginal information gain score for unit i
how much the model attends to unit i when answering the query
how much unit i overlaps in meaning with other units in the context

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose group A: relevance 90%, redundancy 20%. MIG = 90 - 20 = 70.
Group A scores much higher because it is both relevant AND unique.
Group A gets assigned lower compression (keep more tokens); Group B compresses harder.
Under a 32x compression budget, Group A might keep 3% of tokens, Group B only 0.1%, balancing relevance and redundancy loss.

math.note: Subtracting redundancy from relevance ensures we keep tokens that are both important and non-repetitive.

charts.title: Naive compression (relevance only)
charts.note: Keeping only relevance misses the redundancy problem, so the same idea survives multiple times.

charts.title: COMI (relevance minus redundancy)
charts.note: MIG identifies tokens that are both relevant and unique, preserving information with less waste.

items.html: If two pieces of text say the same thing in very different wording, the redundancy score might miss the overlap. This means you keep both copies by accident.

items.b: Grouping by fixed size is rigid.
items.html: The coarse stage divides the document into equal-sized chunks. A chunk might cross a semantic boundary, so the group contains mixed high- and low-value content. The method then assigns one compression rate to both, which is suboptimal.
When compressing by 32x or more, small errors in MIG estimation compound. A token marked as low-redundancy but actually redundant will be kept and waste space.

Use embeddings (dense vectors representing meaning) to measure redundancy rather than word overlap. Estimate groups by looking at semantic breaks, not just fixed size. Validate MIG scores on a held-out set before committing to compression.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple experiment: take a long document (e.g., a Wikipedia article) and a factual question about it. Compress the document to 1/32 its original size using only relevance (naive), then using COMI (relevance minus redundancy). Feed both compressed versions to a language model and ask the question. Measure the accuracy of the answer.
demo.metric_eq: Exact Match accuracy = (model answers correctly with compressed context) / (total questions)
demo.closing: The demo must make it obvious that COMI preserves the tokens the model needs for answering the question (by selecting high MIG tokens) and avoids redundant copies (by subtracting overlap), so the model reads 32 times fewer tokens but still answers the question correctly.
